answers.q: What is Idaho's gun ballot measure, and how is it going?
answers.a: It's an advisory question, not an initiative: Idaho voters are picking an official state firearm from six options — the Winchester Model 1894 (.30-30), the Winchester Model 1873 'Gun that Won the West' (.44-40), the 1873 Colt Single Action Army 'Peacemaker' (.45 Colt), the M1 Garand (.30-06), the Colt M1911 (.45 ACP) and the Remington Model 700 (.30-06). It got there through House Bill 932 (Rep. Jason Monks, R), which passed the House 68–0 and the Senate 32–0 and was signed by Gov. Little on April 2, 2026. The result binds nobody; the Legislature would still have to pass a law naming the winner. Polymarket had the Winchester 1873 as the favorite at 63% on Election Day. Results: none yet — as of 7:47pm PT the Idaho Secretary of State's results site shows 0 of 26 localities reporting for the state's contests (polls closed at 7pm PT in most of Idaho, 8pm PT in the Panhandle). The lab will update this card when the count starts. Same day, Massachusetts votes on a measure to restrict firearms; Idaho's is the one to honor them.

answers.q: Why the blue tide is persuasion, not turnout (3 of 3): splitting the shift into 'who voted' and 'how they voted'
answers.a: A shift-share decomposition on the 182 tracked counties at least half counted: the Democratic margin there is +11.6 tonight vs. -3.8 for Harris in 2024, a shift of +15.4 points. Hold each county's 2024 vote in place and let only the mix of counties change (who turned out, where): that explains +0.1 points. Hold the mix in place and let each county's own margin change (how people voted): that explains +15.3 points. Essentially all of the tide is within-county movement. Caveat: counties, not voters — a county's electorate can change inside the county and show up here as 'persuasion'; and the early-vote skew applies to both bars.

answers.q: Why the blue tide is persuasion, not turnout (2 of 3): the same counties are voting differently
answers.a: Take every county at least half counted with both parties on the ballot (1,825 of them) and compare the Democratic share of its House vote tonight with Harris's share there in 2024. In Harris-won counties Democrats are taking 69.5% tonight vs. 61.5% for Harris. In Trump-won counties they are taking 42.6% vs. 35.7%. The gain is about 7 to 8 points on both sides of the map: the places didn't change, the voters in them did. Caveat: early-counted mail and early ballots lean Democratic in many states, so both tonight bars will likely settle lower as Election Day ballots are added; the comparison is House vote vs. presidential vote, which exaggerates the shift in seats where one party ran a weak candidate in 2024.

answers.q: Why the blue tide is persuasion, not turnout (1 of 3): who is turning out
answers.a: If a turnout surge in blue places were driving the tide, Harris-won counties would be turning out more than Trump-won counties relative to the last midterm. They aren't. In the 60 tracked counties that report all votes counted, Harris counties have cast 109% of their 2022 vote and Trump counties 116%; against 2024 it is 78% and 82%. Red counties are turning out at least as hard as blue ones. The mix of the electorate hasn't moved either: Harris counties are casting 50.8% of these counties' votes tonight, vs. 52.5% in 2022 and 52.3% in 2024. Caveat: 60 fully counted counties, mostly in Virginia, Kentucky, Florida and Ohio; the lab recomputes this every five minutes.

answers.q: How big is tonight's blue tide compared with every red and blue tide of the last 50 years, measured the same way?
answers.a: Measured as the change in the Democratic margin of the House vote from the previous election: tonight, across the 138 districts on unchanged lines that are at least half counted, Democrats are +15.4 where the same districts were R+2.2 in 2024, a swing of +17.6 points. Nothing since 1976 matches it on the blue side: 2006 was +10.6, 2018 +9.7, 1982 +9.5. The only swing of this size in either direction was the 2010 red wave, −17.4; 1994 was −12.2. Caveat: tonight's number is an early count (59% of those districts' 2024 vote) and early-counted mail and early ballots lean Democratic in most of these states, so expect it to come down as Election Day ballots are added; the historical bars are final national House margins. The lab re-measures it every five minutes.

answers.q: when was the last time we had a Dem gov in Tx
answers.a: Ann Richards, elected in 1990 and in office from January 1991 to January 1995; she lost the 1994 race to George W. Bush. Every governor since has been a Republican: Bush (1995–2000), Rick Perry (2000–2015) and Greg Abbott (2015–present), 31 years and counting. The drought is wider than the governorship: no Democrat has won any statewide office in Texas since 1994. Tonight Gina Hinojosa leads Abbott 55–45 with about two-thirds of the expected vote counted (as of 7:07pm; the race is not called), which would make her the first Democratic governor since Richards.

answers.q: What is the current breakdown of seats in the house and senate
answers.a: Going into tonight Republicans hold the House 218 to 214, with one independent and two vacant seats; 218 is a majority, so Democrats need a net gain of only a few seats. Republicans hold the Senate 53 to 47 (45 Democrats plus 2 independents who vote with them), and Vice President Vance breaks ties. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot tonight; Republicans are defending 22 of those Senate seats, Democrats 13.

answers.q: How many House seats does the president's party usually lose in a midterm? (the long view)
answers.a: Since 1946 the president's party has lost House seats in 18 of 20 midterms, about 26 seats on average. The only gains were 1998 under Clinton (+4) and 2002 under George W. Bush (+8). The biggest losses were 2010 under Obama (-63), 1946 under Truman (-56) and 1994 under Clinton (-54); 2022 under Biden was a small one at -9.

answers.q: Show me a graph of how much the presidents party typically suffers in the midterms.
answers.a: The president's party lost ground in both recent midterms. The Republicans lost about 4.8 points of the two-party House vote from 2016 to 2018 under Trump, and the Democrats lost about 2.8 points from 2020 to 2022 under Biden. These figures come from the national House vote in our data, which only goes back to 2016, so the chart shows two midterms and not a long-run average. No results are in yet tonight, so nothing from 2026 is on the chart. When the count starts, the early numbers will be partial, and big blue counties often count more slowly.

answers.q: How has nationwide turnout in House races changed over the last five elections?
answers.a: House races drew about 128 million votes in 2016, 113 million in 2018, 153 million in 2020, 107 million in 2022 and 148 million in 2024. Midterms run well below presidential years: 2018, the highest-turnout midterm in about a century, still came in 15 million votes under 2016, and 2022 drew about 41 million fewer House votes than 2024. The question tonight is whether 2026 lands closer to 2018 or to 2022.
